content: Polystyrene sulfonate is a medication classified as an electrolyte and is approved by the FDA for the treatment of hyperkalemia, a condition characterized by elevated potassium levels in the blood. Common side effects associated with its use include fecal impaction and ischemic colitis. Adult Indications and Dosage Polystyrene sulfonate is specifically indicated for the management of hyperkalemia. The typical adult dosage ranges from 15 grams (60 mL) to 60 grams (240 mL) of suspension daily. This is usually administered as 15 grams (60 mL) of SPS® Suspension one to four times per day. Each 60 mL of the suspension contains 1500 mg (65 mEq) of sodium. The sodium-potassium exchange efficiency of the resin is approximately 33%, meaning only about one-third of the sodium content is delivered to the body. For smaller children and infants, the dosage should be calculated based on a rate of 1 mEq of potassium per gram of resin. The suspension can be administered orally via a plastic tube into the stomach and may be combined with a diet suitable for patients with renal failure. Alternatively, it can be administered rectally as an enema, although this method is less effective. For adults, the enema dosage typically ranges from 30 grams (120 mL) to 50 grams (200 mL) every six hours. The enema should be retained for as long as possible and followed by a cleansing enema. When administering rectally, a soft, large rubber tube (French 28) is inserted approximately 20 cm into the rectum, with the tip positioned in the sigmoid colon. The suspension is introduced at body temperature via gravity, flushed with 50–100 mL of fluid, and the tube is clamped and left in place. If back leakage occurs, the patient’s hips may be elevated or placed in a knee-chest position temporarily. The suspension should remain in the sigmoid colon for several hours if possible, after which the colon is irrigated with a sodium-free cleansing enema at body temperature to remove the resin. Up to two quarts of flushing solution may be required, and the returns are drained continuously through a Y-tube connection. Careful attention must be paid to the cleansing enema, as the vehicle contains sorbitol. The duration and intensity of therapy depend on the severity and resistance of hyperkalemia. The suspension should not be heated, as this may alter the resin’s exchange properties. Contraindications Polystyrene sulfonate is contraindicated in patients with hypokalemia, a history of hypersensitivity to polystyrene sulfonate resins, obstructive bowel disease, or in neonates when administered orally or rectally. Warnings Serious gastrointestinal complications, including intestinal necrosis (which can be fatal), ischemic colitis, bleeding, and perforation, have been reported with the use of sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Many of these cases involved the concurrent use of sorbitol. Risk factors for gastrointestinal adverse events include prematurity, a history of intestinal disease or surgery, hypovolemia, and renal insufficiency or failure. The concomitant administration of additional sorbitol is not recommended. The drug should only be used in patients with normal bowel function and should be avoided in those who have not had a bowel movement post-surgery. It is also contraindicated in patients at risk of constipation or impaction, including those with a history of impaction, chronic constipation, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemic colitis, vascular intestinal atherosclerosis, previous bowel resection, or bowel obstruction. If constipation develops, the drug should be discontinued. In cases of severe hyperkalemia, where rapid correction is required (e.g., in states of rapid tissue breakdown such as burns or renal failure), sodium polystyrene sulfonate alone may not be sufficient. Severe hypokalemia can occur with sodium polystyrene sulfonate therapy, necessitating frequent monitoring of serum potassium levels. Intracellular potassium deficiency may not always be reflected in serum potassium levels, so the decision to discontinue treatment should be individualized based on the patient’s clinical condition and electrocardiogram (ECG) findings. Early signs of severe hypokalemia include irritability, confusion, and delayed thought processes. ECG changes may include a prolonged QT interval, T wave flattening or inversion, and prominent U waves. Cardiac arrhythmias, such as premature atrial, nodal, and ventricular contractions, as well as supraventricular and ventricular tachycardias, may also occur. Severe hypokalemia can lead to muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not entirely selective for potassium and may also cause the loss of other cations, such as magnesium and calcium. Patients should be monitored for all potential electrolyte disturbances. Systemic alkalosis has been reported when the drug is used in combination with nonabsorbable cation-donating antacids or laxatives, such as magnesium hydroxide or aluminum carbonate. Magnesium hydroxide should not be co-administered with sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Adverse Reactions Adverse effects include gastric irritation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, particularly at high doses. Electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and significant sodium retention may occur, along with their associated clinical manifestations. Diarrhea may occasionally develop. In elderly patients, large doses may lead to fecal impaction. Rare cases of intestinal necrosis and obstruction have been reported, particularly when used in combination with aluminum hydroxide. Other reported adverse events include ischemic colitis, gastrointestinal ulceration or necrosis, and intestinal perforation. Rarely, acute bronchitis or bronchopneumonia has been associated with inhalation of polystyrene sulfonate particles. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is classified as Pregnancy Category C. There are no animal reproduction studies or data on its effects on human pregnancy. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Nursing Mothers: It is unknown whether the drug is excreted in human milk. Caution is advised when administering to nursing women. Pediatric Use: The safety and efficacy of the drug in pediatric patients have not been established. It is contraindicated in neonates, particularly premature infants. Rectal administration in children requires caution to avoid impaction, and adequate volumes of sodium-free cleansing enemas should be used. Geriatric Use: There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in elderly patients. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Overdosage Overdosage may result in significant electrolyte disturbances, including hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia. Clinical signs of hypokalemia include irritability, confusion, delayed thought processes, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Tetany may occur. ECG changes consistent with hypokalemia or hypocalcemia, as well as cardiac arrhythmias, may be observed. Management involves correcting serum electrolyte levels and removing the resin from the gastrointestinal tract using laxatives or enemas. Pharmacology Sodium polystyrene sulfonate acts as a cation-exchange resin. As it passes through the gastrointestinal tract or is retained in the colon after enema administration, sodium ions are partially released and replaced by potassium ions. This exchange primarily occurs in the large intestine. The efficiency of this process is variable and averages around 33%. Electrolyte balance must be closely monitored during treatment. Storage and Handling SPS® Suspension should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with permissible temperature excursions between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). The suspension should be dispensed in a tight container and, if repackaged, stored in a refrigerator and used within 14 days. The suspension must be shaken well before use.
